newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Soft EMU scenario seen over-simplified.
newsitem.headline: Soft EMU scenario seen over-simplified.

text.p: Any judgments over the future strength of a single European currency are at this stage highly speculative, particularly those based on the number of countries joining monetary union in 1999, analysts say.

Although the conventional wisdom is that the euro will be launched on schedule with a large group of members, the notion that this will automatically lead to a soft or weak currency is over simplified.
"I think at some point the markets will question that story," says Tim Stewart, global currency strategist for Morgan Stanley.
"At the moment it's basically a view of where dollar/mark is headed in the short-term."
Implicit in this scenario is an evaluation of credibility. Simply put, the larger the number of initial EMU members the weaker the euro's credibility and vice versa.

While there may be a grain of truth in such a view, EU officials caution that any determination over the euro's value against other leading currencies is currently impossible given a raft of unresolved issues, not least the future policy of a European Central Bank.

Although a larger group of countries may make it more difficult for the ECB to come to swift policy decisions on interest rates -- each country will have a representative on its policy-making board -- the institution's mandate to achieve stable and low inflation provides it with a degree of autonomy that any central banker would envy.
As one senior French policy-maker put: "The main responsiblity of the ECB will be to maintain price stability."

Yet the question of a soft or hard euro has become more urgent in light of the leftward political shift in France and the widening debate within Germany over the flexibility of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria for entry into EMU.

An increasing number of economists and market participants believe that the political will behind EMU is now so strong that it will overcome just about any obstacle. This politicisation of the project in turn weakens its economic underpinnings and dilutes the much sought after credibility with markets, say analysts.

But apart from technical issues such as the makeup of the ECB and the number of EMU participants, some argue that the strength of the euro will be determined by a number of extraneous and unpredictable factors.
The state of Europe's economies and that of United States, for example, will play a critical role. One additional factor will be the degree of budgetary restraint in the EU.

Jim O'Neill, global currency strategist for Goldman Sachs in London, reckons that currency markets are missing the more important fundamental development that might arise over the next year or two -- reduced budgetary tightness in Europe.
"The real message to me of what we've seen lately is that there will be no further genuine tightening of fiscal policy," O'Neill said.

EU governments' increased used of budget gimmickry in order to meet the Maastricht criteria and growing public hostility to further austerity measures all point to the possiblity of higher European interest rates.
Rising European rates could in turn lead to a weaker dollar, adds O'Neill.
In addition to the business cycles in Europe and America, the euro's value will also be impacted by global portfolio shifts, an area where few have a confident assessment.
A recent study by the Bank for International Settlements in Switzerland concluded that there were risks associated with shifting portfolios.

"It is possible that the attraction of a larger supply of euro-denominated assets, which in a portfolio balance framework would push down the value of the euro, could outweigh the attraction of a larger demand, which would push it up," the study said.
